knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational Inequality Associated with a Convex Function and a Maximally Monotone Operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a Hilbert-space variational inequality generated by a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function and a set-valued maximally monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), and let \(B:\mathcal H\to2^{\mathcal H}\) be maximally monotone. The associated variational inequality is to find \(x\in\mathcal H\) such that \((\exists u\in Bx)(\forall y\in\mathcal H)\;\langle x-y,u\rangle+f(x)\leq f(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function f and a maximally monotone operator B on a Hilbert space, find x and some u in Bx such that the inner product of x−y with u plus f(x) is at most f(y) for every y in the space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Sol}=\{x\in\mathcal H\mid(\exists u\in Bx)(\forall y\in\mathcal H),\ \langle x-y,u\rangle+f(x)\leq f(y)\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of solutions for compact cusco variational inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence theorem for a multifunction variational inequality on a nonempty compact convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbf E\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(\Omega:C\rightrightarrows\mathbf E\) be cusco. Then there exist \(x_0\in C\) and \(y_0\in\Omega(x_0)\) such that \(\langle y_0,x-x_0\rangle\ge 0\) for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every cusco multifunction on a nonempty compact convex set has a solution to its variational inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbf E\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x_0\in C\;\exists y_0\in\Omega(x_0)\;\forall x\in C:\ \langle y_0,x-x_0\rangle\ge 0.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection fixed-point representation of a convex variational inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between a constant-field variational inequality and a metric-projection equation in Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $W$ be a Hilbert space, let $\varnothing\ne\mathcal C\subset W$ be closed and convex, and let $P_{\mathcal C}$ be its metric projection. For every $w,y\in W$ and every $\gamma>0$, $$w\in\mathcal C\ \text{and}\ (y,v-w)_W\ge0\quad\forall v\in\mathcal C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=P_{\mathcal C}(w-\gamma y).$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any positive step size, a point satisfies the convex-set variational inequality for the vector y exactly when projecting the point after a step in direction minus y returns the same point.
assumptions_latex: \varnothing\ne\mathcal C\subset W\text{ is closed and convex}
P_{\mathcal C}\text{ is the metric projection onto }\mathcal C
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[w\in\mathcal C\ \land\ (y,v-w)_W\ge0\ \forall v\in\mathcal C\right]\iff w-P_{\mathcal C}(w-\gamma y)=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of solutions for coercive noncompact cusco variational inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence theorem replacing compactness of the feasible set with the stated coercivity condition on the multifunction-plus-normal-cone mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbf E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(\Omega:C\rightrightarrows\mathbf E\) be cusco. If \[\liminf_{\substack{\|x\|\to\infty\\x\in C}}\inf_{z\in\Omega(x)+N_C(x)}\langle x,z\rangle>0,\] then there exist \(x_0\in C\) and \(y_0\in\Omega(x_0)\) such that \(\langle y_0,x-x_0\rangle\ge 0\) for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cusco multifunction on a nonempty closed convex set has a variational-inequality solution when the stated normal-cone coercivity condition holds at infinity.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbf E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x_0\in C\;\exists y_0\in\Omega(x_0)\;\forall x\in C:\ \langle y_0,x-x_0\rangle\ge 0.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projected-gradient representation of first-order constrained optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space variational optimality represented as a metric-projection fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $W$ be a Hilbert space, let $\varnothing\ne\mathcal C\subset W$ be closed and convex, and let $J$ be defined on an open neighborhood of $\mathcal C$. If $\bar w$ is a local minimizer and $J$ is Gâteaux differentiable at $\bar w$, then for every $\gamma>0$, $$\bar w=P_{\mathcal C}\bigl(\bar w-\gamma\nabla J(\bar w)\bigr).$$ More generally, this fixed-point equation is equivalent to $$\bar w\in\mathcal C,\qquad \langle J'(\bar w),w-\bar w\rangle_{W^*,W}\ge0\quad\forall w\in\mathcal C.$$ Consequently, under the additional convexity, strict-convexity, or reflexive-space coercivity hypotheses of the corresponding variational-inequality theorem, the fixed-point equation respectively yields global sufficiency, uniqueness, or existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable local minimizer over a nonempty closed convex set is a projected-gradient fixed point for every positive step size. The fixed-point equation is equivalent to the first-order variational inequality and therefore has the same stated convex optimality consequences.
assumptions_latex: \varnothing\ne\mathcal C\subset W\text{ is closed and convex}
J\text{ is defined on an open neighborhood of }\mathcal C
J\text{ is Gâteaux differentiable at }\bar w
\nabla J(\bar w)\text{ is the Riesz representative of }J'(\bar w)
\text{For necessity: }\bar w\text{ is a local minimizer over }\mathcal C
\text{For the additional conclusions: the corresponding convexity, strict-convexity, or reflexive coercivity hypotheses hold}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar w=P_{\mathcal C}(\bar w-\gamma\nabla J(\bar w))\iff\left[\bar w\in\mathcal C\ \land\ \langle J'(\bar w),w-\bar w\rangle_{W^*,W}\ge0\ \forall w\in\mathcal C\right].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear variational inequality induced by a bilinear form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bilinear-form variational inequality on a closed convex subset of a Hilbert space; excludes the extract's unsupported projection interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $V$ be a Hilbert space, let $K\subset V$ be closed and convex, let $a:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be a continuous bilinear form, and let $F\in V'$. The associated linear variational inequality is to find $w\in K$ such that
\[
a(w,v-w)\ge F(v-w)\qquad\text{for every }v\in K.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a closed convex set, a continuous bilinear form, and a continuous linear functional, the linear variational inequality seeks a point w in the set satisfying the variational inequality for every feasible comparison point.
assumptions_latex: K\subset V\text{ is closed and convex}
a:V\times V\to\mathbb R\text{ is continuous and bilinear}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Find }w\in K\text{ such that }\forall v\in K:\ a(w,v-w)\ge F(v-w).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational-inequality characterization of constrained minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order necessity for Gâteaux-differentiable minimization on a convex set, with convexity providing sufficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a real Banach space \(U\), and let \(f\) be real-valued and Gâteaux differentiable on an open set containing \(C\). If \(\bar u\in C\) minimizes \(f\) over \(C\), then \(f'(\bar u)(u-\bar u)\ge 0\) for all \(u\in C\). Conversely, if \(\bar u\in C\) satisfies this inequality and \(f\) is convex, then \(\bar u\) minimizes \(f\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every constrained minimizer satisfies the derivative variational inequality. For a convex objective, the same inequality is sufficient for global optimality.
assumptions_latex: U\text{ is a real Banach space}
f\text{ is real-valued and Gâteaux differentiable on an open set containing }C
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar u\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in C}f(u)\Rightarrow f'(\bar u)(u-\bar u)\ge0\ \forall u\in C;\quad f\text{ convex and }f'(\bar u)(u-\bar u)\ge0\ \forall u\in C\Rightarrow\bar u\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in C}f(u)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compact Convex Solution Set of a Pseudomonotone Variational Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and geometry of the solution set for the displayed Stampacchia variational inequality; condition (4.22) is retained by reference because its content is not included in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that \(h\) is continuous and pseudomonotone on \(X\), and that condition \((4.22)\) holds. Then the variational inequality of finding \(z\in X\) such that \((x-z)^\top h(z)\geq 0\) for every \(x\in X\) has a nonempty, compact, convex solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If h is continuous and pseudomonotone on X and condition (4.22) holds, then the displayed Stampacchia variational inequality has a nonempty, compact, convex solution set.
assumptions_latex: h\text{ is continuous and pseudomonotone on }X
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{z\in X:(x-z)^\top h(z)\geq 0\ \forall x\in X\}\text{ is nonempty, compact, and convex}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(x^*\in C\) solves the Minty variational inequality for \(F\) on \(C\) precisely when
\[\langle F(y),y-x^*\rangle\ge 0\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.\]
Thus the operator is evaluated at each comparison point \(y\), rather than at \(x^*\). The solution set is denoted by \(\operatorname{SOL}_M(F,C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Minty solution pairs the operator at every comparison point with its displacement from the candidate and requires all pairings to be nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.title: Minty Variational Inequality

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Correspondence Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone, segment-hemicontinuous Hilbert-space correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq H\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(F:C\to H\). Assume that \(\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\ge 0\) for every \(x,y\in C\), and that for every \(x,y\in C\) the map \(t\mapsto\langle F(x+t(y-x)),y-x\rangle\), defined for \(t\in[0,1]\), is right-continuous at \(t=0\). Then, for every \(x^*\in C\),
\[x^*\in\operatorname{SOL}_S(F,C)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x^*\in\operatorname{SOL}_M(F,C).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a monotone operator that is right-continuous along feasible segments, the Stampacchia and Minty solution sets coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty and convex.
\(F:C\to H\) is monotone and right-continuous at the initial point of every segment in \(C\) in the stated scalar-pairing sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{SOL}_S(F,C)=\operatorname{SOL}_M(F,C)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudomonotone Correspondence Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise pseudomonotonicity with segment hemicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq H\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(F:C\to H\). Assume that, for every \(x,y\in C\),
\[\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\ge0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\langle F(y),y-x\rangle\ge0,\]
and that the map \(t\mapsto\langle F(x+t(y-x)),y-x\rangle\), defined for \(t\in[0,1]\), is right-continuous at \(t=0\). Then, for every \(x^*\in C\),
\[x^*\in\operatorname{SOL}_S(F,C)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x^*\in\operatorname{SOL}_M(F,C).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a pointwise pseudomonotone operator that is right-continuous along feasible segments, the Stampacchia and Minty solution sets coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty and convex.
\(F:C\to H\) satisfies the displayed pointwise pseudomonotonicity implication and segment right-continuity condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{SOL}_S(F,C)=\operatorname{SOL}_M(F,C)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(C=[0,1]\) and \(F(x)=1-2x\), direct evaluation of
\[F(x^*)(y-x^*)\ge0\qquad(y\in C)\]
gives \(\operatorname{SOL}_S(F,C)=\{0,\tfrac12,1\}\). In contrast, the Minty inequalities \(F(y)(y-x^*)\ge0\) force \(x^*\le0\) from \(y<\tfrac12\) and \(x^*\ge1\) from \(y>\tfrac12\), with incompatible endpoint inequalities; thus \(\operatorname{SOL}_M(F,C)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decreasing affine operator on an interval has three Stampacchia solutions but no Minty solution, showing that nonmonotonicity can separate the concepts.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone Solution-Concept Separation

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(N_C(x)=\{v\in H:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }y\in C\}\) for \(x\in C\). Then \(x^*\in C\) solves the Stampacchia VI exactly when
\[0\in F(x^*)+N_C(x^*).\]
Because \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, this is also equivalent, for every \(\lambda>0\), to
\[x^*=P_C\bigl(x^*-\lambda F(x^*)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a closed convex set, a VI is equivalently a normal-cone inclusion or a fixed point of a projected operator step.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex-Set VIs

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(x^*\in C\) solves the Stampacchia VI if and only if there exists \(\lambda^*\in\mathbb R^m\) such that
\[F(x^*)+A^{\mathsf T}\lambda^*=0,\qquad \lambda^*\ge0,\qquad Ax^*\le b,\qquad \lambda^*\odot(Ax^*-b)=0.\]
Thus a VI over a polyhedron has a finite multiplier and complementarity representation, including redundant inequality descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A VI on an inequality-defined polyhedron is equivalent to stationarity, primal feasibility, nonnegative multipliers, and complementary slackness.

knowledge_statements.title: Box-Constrained VIs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite box with coordinatewise characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), let \(C=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\subset\mathbb R^n\), where \(-\infty<\ell_i<u_i<\infty\), and let \(F:C\to\mathbb R^n\). A point \(x^*\in C\) solves the Stampacchia variational inequality if and only if, for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\),
\[\begin{cases}F_i(x^*)\ge0,&x_i^*=\ell_i,\\F_i(x^*)=0,&\ell_i<x_i^*<u_i,\\F_i(x^*)\le0,&x_i^*=u_i.\end{cases}\]
These conditions are equivalent to \(0\in F(x^*)+N_C(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite box, each operator component is nonnegative at its lower bound, zero in the coordinate interior, and nonpositive at its upper bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\) solves the VI exactly when every coordinate satisfies the displayed bound-dependent sign condition.

The box has the polyhedral representation
\[C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:x_i\le u_i,
\ -x_i\le-\ell_i\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,n\}.\]
For \(x\in C\), its normal cone is
\[N_C(x)=\operatorname{cone}\bigl(\{e_i:x_i=u_i\}\cup\{-e_i:x_i=\ell_i\}\bigr).\]
Consequently, box-constrained VIs are polyhedral VIs whose active constraint normals are signed coordinate vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite box is a bounded polyhedron, and its normal cone is generated by signed coordinate vectors at active bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Box Geometry as a Polyhedral Specialization

knowledge_statements.title: Cartesian-Product VIs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite Cartesian products of real Hilbert spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\in\mathbb N\), let \(H_i\) be a real Hilbert space, and let \(C_i\subseteq H_i\) be nonempty for each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Equip \(H=H_1\times\cdots\times H_m\) with its canonical product inner product, set \(C=C_1\times\cdots\times C_m\), and let \(F=(F_1,\ldots,F_m):C\to H\). For \(x^*=(x_1^*,\ldots,x_m^*)\in C\),
\[\sum_{i=1}^m\langle F_i(x^*),y_i-x_i^*\rangle_{H_i}\ge0\qquad\text{for every }y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)\in C\]
holds if and only if, for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\),
\[\langle F_i(x^*),z_i-x_i^*\rangle_{H_i}\ge0\qquad\text{for every }z_i\in C_i.\]
Each \(F_i(x^*)\) may depend on the full vector \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variational inequality on a finite Cartesian product of Hilbert spaces is equivalent to one inequality per block, while each block operator may depend on all blocks.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb N\), each \(H_i\) is a real Hilbert space, and each \(C_i\subseteq H_i\) is nonempty.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The operator \(F\) is monotone on \(C\) when
\[\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.\]
This definition permits equality for distinct points; strict monotonicity instead requires a strict inequality whenever \(x\ne y\). No continuity, convexity of \(C\), or maximality is included in monotonicity itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator is monotone when differences of its values have nonnegative inner product with the corresponding differences of points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict monotonicity, strict feasibility, and uniqueness for cone complementarity problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A complementarity specialization of the solution-geometry consequences of strict monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be a pointed, closed, convex cone and let F:K\to\mathbb{R}^n be continuous. Then
\[
\bigl[F\text{ is strictly monotone on }K\text{ and }\operatorname{FEA}(K,F)\neq\varnothing\bigr]
\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl[F\text{ is strictly monotone on }K\text{ and }\operatorname{CP}(K,F)\text{ is strictly feasible}\bigr],
\]
and either equivalent condition implies that \(\operatorname{CP}(K,F)\) has a unique solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous map on a pointed closed convex cone, strict monotonicity with nonempty feasibility is equivalent to strict monotonicity with strict feasibility of the complementarity problem, and either condition implies uniqueness of its solution.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard inverse-strong-monotonicity convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The operator \(F\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive on \(C\), for \(\beta>0\), if
\[\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\geq \beta\|F(x)-F(y)\|^2\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.\]
In particular, every cocoercive operator is monotone and is \(1/\beta\)-Lipschitz on \(C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathcal H\) be nonempty, let \(T:D\to\mathcal H\), let \(\beta>0\), and let \(\gamma\in(0,2\beta)\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The VI operator \(F\) is integrable, or a potential operator, on \(U\) if there exists a continuously differentiable function \(\phi:U\to\mathbb R\) satisfying
\[F(x)=\nabla\phi(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.\]
The function \(\phi\) is determined up to an additive constant on each connected component of \(U\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is no \(\phi\in C^2(\mathbb R^2)\) satisfying \(F=\nabla\phi\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rotation field as a canonical smooth nonpotential operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F(x_1,x_2)=(-x_2,x_1)\), the Jacobian is
\[DF(x)=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\]
which is not symmetric. If \(F=\nabla\phi\) for some \(\phi\in C^2(\mathbb R^2)\), then \(DF=\nabla^2\phi\) would be symmetric. Therefore this smooth VI operator admits no twice continuously differentiable scalar potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The planar rotation field is nonpotential: its nonsymmetric Jacobian cannot be the Hessian of a twice continuously differentiable scalar function.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonpotential VI Operators

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is monotone on \(C\) if and only if \(\langle Mz,z\rangle\ge 0\) for every \(z\in C-C\); it is monotone on all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) if and only if \(M+M^\mathsf{T}\succeq0\).

notation.meaning: The affine operator defining the VI.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity conditions for a finite-dimensional affine VI operator, distinguishing monotonicity on the feasible set from global monotonicity.

source_refs.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The affine field \(F(x)=Mx+q\) is monotone on \(C\) when
\[
\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\ge0
\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.
\]
Equivalently, it is monotone on \(C\) if and only if
\[
\langle Mz,z\rangle\ge0
\qquad\text{for every }z\in C-C.
\]
If monotonicity is required on all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), this holds if and only if the symmetric part \(\tfrac12(M+M^\mathsf{T})\) is positive semidefinite, equivalently \(M+M^\mathsf{T}\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine field is monotone on the feasible set when its quadratic form is nonnegative on every feasible difference. Global monotonicity is equivalent to positive semidefiniteness of the symmetric part of its linear term, and the constant term has no effect.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone AVIs

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter III. Variational Inequalities for Monotone Operators p. 83

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common invariants of monotone AVI solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantities constant across all solutions of a nonempty positive-semidefinite affine variational inequality, with a KKT identity in the polyhedral case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be closed and convex, let q\in\mathbb{R}^n, let M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be positive semidefinite, and suppose \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,q,M)\neq\varnothing\). There exist d\in\mathbb{R}^n and \(\sigma\geq0\) such that every x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,q,M) satisfies
\[
(M+M^T)x=d,\qquad x^TMx=\sigma.
\]
If additionally \(K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq b\}\) is polyhedral and \((x,\lambda)\) is any KKT pair of the AVI, then
\[
\sigma+q^Tx+b^T\lambda=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All solutions of a nonempty positive-semidefinite affine variational inequality share the same image under the symmetric part of the matrix and the same quadratic value. In the stated polyhedral representation, every KKT pair also satisfies the scalar identity.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the final identity: }K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq b\}\text{ and }(x,\lambda)\text{ is a KKT pair}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists d\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ \exists\sigma\geq0,\ \forall x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,q,M):\ (M+M^T)x=d,\ x^TMx=\sigma;\quad K\text{ polyhedral and }(x,\lambda)\text{ KKT}\Longrightarrow\sigma+q^Tx+b^T\lambda=0

children.title: Conic Monotone AVI Intersection
children.top_down_role: The regime where conic feasibility coexists with affine monotonicity.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{SOL}(K,Mx+q)\) is the conic complementarity solution set of a monotone affine field.

notation.meaning: The symmetric part of M is positive semidefinite.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: this node is the literal intersection of the conic and monotone AVI subclasses
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intersection of conic affine VIs and globally monotone affine VIs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A conic monotone affine variational inequality is the conic AVI
\[
\text{find }x^\star\in K\text{ such that }\langle Mx^\star+q,y-x^\star\rangle\ge0
\quad\text{for every }y\in K,
\]
with the additional monotonicity condition \(M+M^\mathsf{T}\succeq0\). Equivalently, it is the monotone conic complementarity system
\[
x^\star\in K,
\qquad Mx^\star+q\in K^*,
\qquad \langle x^\star,Mx^\star+q\rangle=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This class contains exactly the conic AVIs whose affine field is monotone, equivalently whose matrix has positive-semidefinite symmetric part.
knowledge_statements.title: Conic Monotone AVI Intersection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly describes the intersection of conic and globally monotone affine VIs, and definition is an appropriate knowledge kind for this class leaf. It nevertheless lacks a citation and specific locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional set-valued generalized VI with fixed convex feasibility set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set-valued generalized variational inequality for \(T\) and \(C\) is to find \(x^\star\in C\) and \(u^\star\in T(x^\star)\) such that
\[
\langle u^\star,y-x^\star\rangle\ge0
\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
With \(N_C(x)=\{v:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }y\in C\}\), existence of such a selection \(u^\star\) is equivalent to
\[
0\in T(x^\star)+N_C(x^\star).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-valued GVI selects a field value at the unknown point that satisfies the usual VI inequality, equivalently a normal-cone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Valued GVIs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The existential-selection GVI and normal-cone inclusion are consistent with the stated normal-cone convention, but the record supplies no inspectable source.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(H\) are real Hilbert spaces, and \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(F:X\to H\) and \(g:X\to H\) are given mappings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\) is a solution exactly when \(0\in F(x^\star)+N_C(g(x^\star))\).

notation.meaning: The mapping through which feasibility is imposed.
The normal cone to C at g(x).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the transformed-point convention; other literature uses state-dependent feasible-set conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the transformed-point convention, an implicit variational inequality seeks \(x^\star\in X\) such that \(g(x^\star)\in C\) and
\[
\langle F(x^\star),y-g(x^\star)\rangle_H\ge0
\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
Equivalently, with the Hilbert-space normal cone to \(C\), the defining inclusion is
\[
0\in F(x^\star)+N_C(g(x^\star)).
\]
The ordinary VI is recovered when \(X=H\) and \(g\) is the identity mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An implicit VI imposes the variational inequality at a transformed point, with both the field and transformation depending on the unknown.
knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Variational Inequalities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The transformed-point formulation is internally coherent, but 'implicit variational inequality' has multiple non-equivalent conventions. A source specifically supporting this convention is required before the mathematical version can be accepted.

notation.meaning: The normal cone to the realized feasible set K(x).

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: state-dependent feasibility is the defining QVI feature
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface definition only; existence, stability, and algorithms for state-dependent feasible sets are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The quasi-variational inequality determined by \(F\) and the feasible-set mapping \(K\) is to find \(x^\star\in H\) such that
\[
x^\star\in K(x^\star)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle_H\ge0
\qquad\text{for every }y\in K(x^\star).
\]
Equivalently, the state-dependent normal-cone formulation is
\[
0\in F(x^\star)+N_{K(x^\star)}(x^\star),
\qquad x^\star\in K(x^\star).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasi-VI is a VI whose feasible set depends on the unknown point itself.
knowledge_statements.title: Quasi-Variational Inequalities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The state-dependent feasible-set definition is precise, matches the interface-only scope, and uses an appropriate definition container, but no citation with a locator is present.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\iff\bigl[x\in\operatorname{dom}K\ \text{and}\ \mathbf F_K^{\mathrm{nat}}(x)=0\bigr]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quasi-variational inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-dependent feasible-set extension of a variational inequality, including the zero-field fixed-point specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) be a point-to-set map, possibly with empty values, and let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\). The quasi-variational inequality defined by \((K,F)\) is to find \(x\) such that \[x\in K(x),\qquad (y-x)^TF(x)\geq0\quad\forall y\in K(x).\] If \(F\equiv0\), it reduces to finding a fixed point \(x\in K(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasi-variational inequality seeks a point feasible for its own state-dependent feasible set that satisfies the variational inequality over that set. With the zero field, it becomes a fixed-point problem for the set-valued map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in K(x)\ \text{and}\ (y-x)^TF(x)\geq0\ \forall y\in K(x);\qquad F\equiv0\Rightarrow x\in K(x).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract scalar bifunction equilibrium problem on a fixed feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The bifunction equilibrium problem associated with \(f\) and \(C\) is
\[
\text{find }x^\star\in C\text{ such that }f(x^\star,y)\ge0
\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
Thus its solution set is
\[
\operatorname{EP}(f,C)=\{x\in C:f(x,y)\ge0\text{ for every }y\in C\}.
\]
The normalization \(f(x,x)=0\) makes the comparison with the current point neutral and is part of the local convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An equilibrium point makes a scalar bifunction nonnegative against every feasible comparison point.
knowledge_statements.title: Bifunction Equilibrium Problems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalized bifunction equilibrium definition is internally consistent and fits the leaf, but it has no inspectable citation or locator.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x,y)\ge0\Rightarrow f(y,x)\le0\) for all \(x,y\in C\).

notation.meaning: The solution set of the associated equilibrium problem.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selects pseudomonotonicity as the generalized monotonicity notion; terminology varies across sources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the pseudomonotone-bifunction convention, a generalized monotone equilibrium problem is the problem of finding \(x^\star\in C\) such that \(f(x^\star,y)\ge0\) for every \(y\in C\), where
\[
f(x,y)\ge0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(y,x)\le0
\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.
\]
Ordinary monotonicity,
\[
f(x,y)+f(y,x)\le0
dot\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C,
\]
implies this pseudomonotonicity condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the selected convention, generalized monotonicity means pseudomonotonicity of the equilibrium bifunction; ordinary bifunction monotonicity is stronger.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Monotone Equilibrium Problems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selected pseudomonotonicity convention requires source confirmation because generalized monotonicity terminology is not unique. In addition, the displayed ordinary-monotonicity formula contains the stray token 'dot' before \(\qquad\), which must be removed once the convention is sourced.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{VI}(F,C)=\operatorname{EP}(f_F,C)\).

notation.meaning: The VI and equilibrium-problem solution sets.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: substituting the induced bifunction gives literal equality of the defining predicates
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence for the bifunction induced by a single-valued Hilbert-space operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the bifunction induced by \(F\) as
\[
f_F(x,y)=\langle F(x),y-x\rangle_H
\qquad\text{for }x,y\in C.
\]
Then \(f_F(x,x)=0\), and for every \(x^\star\in C\),
\[
\langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle_H\ge0\text{ for every }y\in C
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
f_F(x^\star,y)\ge0\text{ for every }y\in C.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{VI}(F,C)=\operatorname{EP}(f_F,C).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every single-valued VI is exactly an equilibrium problem for the bifunction formed by pairing the operator with feasible displacements.
knowledge_statements.title: VI–Equilibrium Problem Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The induced-bifunction correspondence is exact, the representation knowledge kind fits the leaf, and the plain and LaTeX statements agree. The record still lacks a citation with a specific locator.

children.top_down_role: Expected-value and sample-based models are signposted without importing stochastic approximation theory.

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})\) is a probability space and \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(G:C\times\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is measurable in its random argument and integrable for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in\operatorname{SOL}(C,F)\) with \(F(x)=\mathbb{E}[G(x,\xi)]\).

notation.meaning: A random sample or random element.
The sample-average operator based on N observations.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: expected-value and sample-average VI formulations are standard interfaces
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formulation interface only; stochastic approximation, sampling error, and convergence theory are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The expected-value stochastic VI seeks \(x^\star\in C\) such that
\[
\langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle\ge0
\qquad\text{for every }y\in C,
\quad
F(x)=\mathbb{E}[G(x,\xi)].
\]
Given samples \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N\), its sample-average formulation replaces \(F\) by
\[
F_N(x)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N G(x,\xi_i)
\]
and solves the deterministic VI \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F_N)\). No assertion about consistency or sampling complexity is included.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic VI applies the deterministic VI condition to an expected random field; sample-average models replace that expectation by an empirical mean.
knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic VI Formulation Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The expected-value and sample-average formulations fit the interface scope, but no source is cited. A sourced version should also define the random element \(\xi:\Omega\to\Xi\) and the corresponding domain of the measurable random argument explicitly.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Hilbert-space variational inequality determined by \(F\) and \(C\) is to find \(x^\star\in C\) such that
\[
\langle F(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle_H\ge0
\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
For the normal cone
\[
N_C(x)=\{v\in H:\langle v,y-x\rangle_H\le0\text{ for every }y\in C\},
\]
the VI is equivalent to the inclusion
\[
0\in F(x^\star)+N_C(x^\star).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hilbert-space VI seeks a feasible point where the operator pairs nonnegatively with every feasible displacement.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a real Banach space, let \(C\subset X\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(F:C\to X^*\). The Banach-space variational inequality \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\) asks for \(\bar x\in C\) such that
\[
\langle F(\bar x),y-\bar x\rangle_{X^*,X}\ge 0\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
Here the inequality is scalar and uses the canonical duality pairing. Closedness of \(C\), continuity or monotonicity of \(F\), and geometric properties of \(X\) are additional hypotheses used for existence or algorithmic results, not part of the problem definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Banach-space VI seeks a feasible point whose operator value has nonnegative dual pairing with every feasible displacement.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_C\) denote the Euclidean metric projection onto \(C\). For every \(x\in C\) and every \(\alpha>0\),
\[
x\in\operatorname{SOL}(C,F)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=P_C\bigl(x-\alpha F(x)\bigr).
\]
Equivalently, the VI solution set is the fixed-point set of \(P_C\circ(I-\alpha F)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point solves the Euclidean VI exactly when projecting any positive forward step back onto the feasible set returns that point.
knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Projection Representation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed symmetric positive-definite metric in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the \(H\)-metric projection by \(P_C^H(u)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in C}\tfrac12\|y-u\|_H^2\). For every \(x\in C\) and \(\alpha>0\),
\[
x\in\operatorname{SOL}(C,F)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x=P_C^H\bigl(x-\alpha H^{-1}F(x)\bigr).
\]
The weighted projection condition is \(\langle H(x-u),y-x\rangle\ge0\) for every \(y\in C\). Substitution of \(u=x-\alpha H^{-1}F(x)\) reduces it to \(\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\ge0\) for every \(y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The VI is equivalently a fixed-point equation for projection in any fixed positive-definite metric, with the operator step scaled by the inverse metric.
knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Metric Projection Representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed positive-definite metric formula is mathematically standard and internally consistent, but no inspectable source with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator is supplied. The statement also contains a derivation that must be removed after sourcing.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(T:C\to C\) by \(T(x)=P_C(x-\alpha F(x))\) and set \(q=\sqrt{1-2\alpha\mu+\alpha^2L^2}\). Then \(0\le q<1\) and
\[
\|T(x)-T(y)\|\le q\|x-y\|\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.
\]
The map \(T\) has a unique fixed point \(x^*\in C\), which is the unique solution of \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\). Moreover, for every \(x^0\in C\), the iteration \(x^{k+1}=T(x^k)\) satisfies
\[
\|x^k-x^*\|\le q^k\|x^0-x^*\|.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the strongly monotone and Lipschitz Euclidean regime, a suitable projected forward step is contractive, has the unique VI solution as its fixed point, and converges globally at a linear rate bounded by its contraction factor.
knowledge_statements.title: Contractive Fixed-Point Regime

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Averaged-operator regime without a strict contraction assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(F\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive, meaning
\[
\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\ge\beta\|F(x)-F(y)\|^2
\]
for all \(x,y\in C\). For \(0<\alpha<2\beta\), the forward map \(I-\alpha F\) is averaged, and its composition with the firmly nonexpansive projection \(P_C\) is averaged. Hence \(T=P_C\circ(I-\alpha F)\) is nonexpansive but need not have Lipschitz modulus strictly below one. Nevertheless,
\[
\operatorname{Fix}T=\operatorname{SOL}(C,F).
\]
Thus fixed-point algorithms based on averagedness apply even when Banach contraction theory does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cocoercivity makes the projected forward map averaged and nonexpansive; its fixed points remain exactly the VI solutions even without strict contraction.
knowledge_statements.title: Noncontractive Fixed-Point Representations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The averaged-operator conclusion is plausible and standard, but no source is supplied. A source is also needed to confirm the precise domain convention under which the composition is asserted to be averaged, since the assumptions do not explicitly declare a map \(F:C\to H\) or an extension to the ambient Hilbert space.

source_refs.locator: I.4 Variational Inequalities p. 13
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(N_C(x)=\{v\in H:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }y\in C\}\) for \(x\in C\), and \(N_C(x)=\varnothing\) otherwise. Then
\[
x\in\operatorname{SOL}(C,F)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
-F(x)\in N_C(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0\in F(x)+N_C(x).
\]
Thus the feasible-set constraint and all VI test inequalities are encoded by the normal-cone operator. The equivalence is algebraic and does not require monotonicity of \(F\); monotonicity becomes relevant to the properties and solution methods of the resulting inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The VI is exactly the zero-inclusion problem obtained by adding the feasible set's normal cone to the original operator.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Inclusion Reformulation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-resolvent representation of a two-operator inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\gamma>0\), define the resolvent \(J_{\gamma A}=(I+\gamma A)^{-1}\). Then
\[
0\in A(x)+B(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x=J_{\gamma A}\bigl(x-\gamma B(x)\bigr).
\]
A constrained VI is recovered by taking \(A=N_C\) and \(B=F\), in which case \(J_{\gamma N_C}=P_C\). More generally, choosing \(A=\partial g+N_C\) separates nonsmooth and constraint structure from the explicit field \(B\). The equivalence itself requires only the resolvent definition; additional cocoercivity or Lipschitz assumptions govern convergence of forward-backward iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Splitting the VI operator into implicit and explicit parts turns its zero inclusion into a resolvent fixed-point equation suitable for operator splitting.
knowledge_statements.title: Structured Operator-Sum Reformulation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The resolvent equivalence is mathematically correct, and the extra monotonicity assumptions do not invalidate it, but the record has no inspectable citation. A section, proposition, theorem, definition, or page locator supporting the resolvent identity is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\alpha>0\), define the natural map on \(\mathbb R^n\) by
\[
R_\alpha(x)=x-P_C\bigl(x-\alpha F(x)\bigr).
\]
Then
\[
R_\alpha(x)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x=P_C\bigl(x-\alpha F(x)\bigr)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x\in\operatorname{SOL}(C,F).
\]
In particular, any zero is automatically feasible because it equals a point in the range of \(P_C\). Thus the constrained variational inequality is represented by the unconstrained nonsmooth equation \(R_\alpha(x)=0\), and \(\|R_\alpha(x)\|\) is a residual vanishing exactly at solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting the projected forward step from the current point gives a natural residual whose zeros coincide exactly with VI solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Natural-Map Equation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unscaled Euclidean normal map for a polyhedral feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the normal map
\[
F_C(z)=F(P_Cz)+z-P_Cz,
\qquad z\in\mathbb R^n.
\]
If \(F_C(z)=0\) and \(x=P_Cz\), then \(z-x=-F(x)\in N_C(x)\), so \(x\in\operatorname{SOL}(C,F)\). Conversely, if \(x\) solves the VI, then \(z=x-F(x)\) satisfies \(P_Cz=x\) and \(F_C(z)=0\). For polyhedral \(C\), the projection \(P_C\) is piecewise affine on a finite polyhedral subdivision. Consequently, when \(F\) is affine, the normal map \(F_C\) is piecewise affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polyhedral normal map converts the VI into an equation; affine fields yield a piecewise-affine equation because projection onto a polyhedron is piecewise affine.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Normal Maps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated zero correspondence and the piecewise-affine conclusion for affine fields over a polyhedral set are standard, but no source with a specific locator is supplied. The candidate also contains a derivation that must be removed once a supporting source is identified.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar-scaled Euclidean normal map; no smoothing of the projection is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a parameter \(\rho>0\), define
\[
F_{C,\rho}(z)=F(P_Cz)+\rho^{-1}(z-P_Cz).
\]
If \(F_{C,\rho}(z)=0\) and \(x=P_Cz\), then \(z-x=-\rho F(x)\in N_C(x)\), because the normal cone is positively homogeneous; hence \(x\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\). Conversely, if \(x\) solves the VI, then \(z=x-\rho F(x)\) satisfies \(P_Cz=x\) and \(F_{C,\rho}(z)=0\). Thus every positive scaling preserves the solution correspondence while changing the equation's scaling and potentially its numerical conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive scaling of the normal correction preserves the exact correspondence between normal-map zeros and VI solutions while changing numerical conditioning.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularized Normal Maps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive scaling preserves the normal-map zero correspondence, but no source is supplied and the label 'regularized normal map' is not established by the record. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean normal map for a parameter-dependent convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(p\in P\) and \(z\in\mathbb R^n\), the parametric normal map associated with \(F\) and \(C\) is
\[
M(p,z):=F\bigl(p,\Pi_{C(p)}z\bigr)+z-\Pi_{C(p)}z.
\]
Writing \(x:=\Pi_{C(p)}z\), the projection characterization gives \(z-x\in N_{C(p)}(x)\). Consequently,
\[
M(p,z)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
-F(p,x)\in N_{C(p)}(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\langle F(p,x),y-x\rangle\geq0\quad\text{for every }y\in C(p).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameterized VI is equivalent to finding a zero of the normal map formed from its field and the projector onto its parameterized feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Normal Maps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normal-map formula and VI equivalence are mathematically standard and fit the leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied. The explanatory transition also reads as proof text and should be removed when sourced.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The variational inequality
\[
\langle \nabla f(x^*),x-x^*\rangle\geq0\quad\text{for every }x\in C
\]
is equivalent to \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\). Under the stated constraint qualification, this is further equivalent to the existence of multipliers \(\lambda_i\geq0\) and \(\mu_j\in\mathbb R\) such that
\[
\nabla f(x^*)+\sum_i\lambda_i\nabla g_i(x^*)+\sum_j\mu_j\nabla h_j(x^*)=0,
\quad g_i(x^*)\leq0,
\quad h_j(x^*)=0,
\quad \lambda_i g_i(x^*)=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the VI field is a convex potential gradient, the VI is convex minimization and, under Slater's condition, reduces exactly to its KKT system.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrable-VI KKT Reduction

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-System KKT Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex constraint systems satisfying Slater's condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_i(x)\leq0\ (i=1,\ldots,q),\ h_j(x)=0\ (j=1,\ldots,r)\}.
\]
A point \(x^*\in C\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\) if and only if there exist \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^q\) and \(\mu\in\mathbb R^r\) such that
\[
F(x^*)+\sum_{i=1}^q\lambda_i\nabla g_i(x^*)+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\nabla h_j(x^*)=0,
\qquad
\lambda_i g_i(x^*)=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,q).
\]
Primal feasibility is expressed by \(x^*\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex differentiable constraint system satisfying Slater's condition, the VI is equivalent to primal feasibility, stationarity, nonnegative inequality multipliers, unrestricted equality multipliers, and complementary slackness.
assumptions_latex: For \(i=1,\ldots,q\), \(g_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is convex and continuously differentiable.
The set \(C\) is nonempty and satisfies Slater's condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\) exactly when it admits multipliers satisfying the displayed KKT system.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order VI representation of finite-dimensional differentiable convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x^*\in C\),
\[
x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\langle\nabla f(x^*),x-x^*\rangle\geq0
\quad\text{for every }x\in C.
\]
Thus the optimization problem is represented by \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\) with \(F:=\nabla f\), equivalently by
\[
0\in\nabla f(x^*)+N_C(x^*).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Differentiable convex minimization over a closed convex set is equivalent to the VI whose field is the objective gradient.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Obstacle variational inequality as constrained energy minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of the elliptic obstacle variational inequality and a strictly convex quadratic minimization problem, together with uniqueness and the stated regularity conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q\in[2,\infty)\), let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2\) be nonempty, bounded, open, and have sufficiently smooth boundary, let \(g\in W^{2,q}(\Omega)\) satisfy \(g\le 0\) on \(\partial\Omega\), and let \(f\in L^q(\Omega)\). Let \(a:H_0^1(\Omega)\times H_0^1(\Omega)\to\mathbb R\) be a bounded symmetric bilinear form satisfying \(a(z,z)\ge \nu\lVert z\rVert_{H_0^1}^2\) for every \(z\in H_0^1(\Omega)\), where \(\nu>0\). Define \(\mathcal F=\{z\in H_0^1(\Omega):z\ge g\text{ on }\Omega\}\) and \(J(z)=\tfrac12a(z,z)-(f,z)_{L^2}\). Then \(y\in\mathcal F\) satisfies \(a(y,v-y)-(f,v-y)_{L^2}\ge0\) for every \(v\in\mathcal F\) if and only if \(y\) minimizes \(J\) over \(\mathcal F\). Since \(\mathcal F\) is closed and convex and \(J\) is strictly convex and coercive, the problem has a unique solution \(\bar y\). Under the elliptic regularity result invoked for these data and coefficients, \(\bar y\in H_0^1(\Omega)\cap W^{2,q}(\Omega)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The elliptic obstacle variational inequality is equivalent to minimizing its quadratic energy over the closed convex obstacle set. Ellipticity makes the energy strictly convex and coercive, yielding a unique solution; the invoked elliptic regularity result gives W^{2,q} regularity.
assumptions_latex: \varnothing\ne\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2\text{ is bounded and open with sufficiently smooth boundary}
a:H_0^1(\Omega)\times H_0^1(\Omega)\to\mathbb R\text{ is bounded, symmetric, and }a(z,z)\ge\nu\lVert z\rVert_{H_0^1}^2\ \forall z\in H_0^1(\Omega)\text{ for some }\nu>0
\mathcal F=\{z\in H_0^1(\Omega):z\ge g\text{ on }\Omega\}\text{ is closed and convex}
\text{The elliptic regularity result cited in the source applies to the stated domain, coefficients, and data}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y\text{ solves the obstacle VI}\iff y\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in\mathcal F}J(z),\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in\mathcal F}J(z)=\{\bar y\},\qquad \bar y\in H_0^1(\Omega)\cap W^{2,q}(\Omega).

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) are nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable, convex in \(x\), and concave in \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A pair is a saddle point of \(L\) exactly when it solves the VI on \(X\times Y\) with field \((\nabla_xL,-\nabla_yL)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional convex-concave saddle problems.

source_refs.locator: I.5 Some Problems Which Lead to Variational Inequalities p. 15
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Variational Inequalities and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A pair \((x^*,y^*)\in X\times Y\) is a saddle point when
\[
L(x^*,y)\leq L(x^*,y^*)\leq L(x,y^*)
\quad\text{for every }(x,y)\in X\times Y.
\]
Under convexity-concavity, this is equivalent to
\[
\left\langle\nabla_xL(x^*,y^*),x-x^*\right\rangle
-\left\langle\nabla_yL(x^*,y^*),y-y^*\right\rangle\geq0
\quad\text{for every }(x,y)\in X\times Y,
\]
which is \(\operatorname{VI}(X\times Y,F)\) for \(F(x,y):=(\nabla_xL(x,y),-\nabla_yL(x,y))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth convex-concave saddle point is precisely a VI solution for the primal gradient and negative dual gradient on the product set.

children.title: Optimization-to-Saddle Reduction Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions between optimization-derived and saddle-derived VI representations.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable, but convexity is not assumed.
Stationarity is encoded as the unconstrained VI \(\nabla f(x^*)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without convexity, the optimization-to-VI or saddle first-order system can contain points that are not minimizers or saddle points.

notation.meaning: Nonconvex objective used in the boundary example

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of converse first-order reductions without convexity-concavity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the unconstrained problem with
\[
f(x):=(x^2-1)^2,
\qquad \nabla f(x)=4x(x^2-1).
\]
The point \(x^*=0\) satisfies the associated variational inequality on \(\mathbb R\), because \(\nabla f(0)=0\). Nevertheless, \(f(0)=1\) while \(f(1)=f(-1)=0\), and \(x^*=0\) is a strict local maximum. Hence a first-order VI, KKT, or degenerate saddle representation is not equivalent to global optimization after convexity is removed. Analogously, without convexity in the primal variable and concavity in the dual variable, saddle-gradient VI solutions need not satisfy the global saddle inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without convexity-concavity, first-order VI or saddle systems may admit stationary points that are neither minimizers nor saddle points.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimization-to-Saddle Reduction Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample correctly demonstrates failure of the optimization-to-VI converse without convexity, but the record supplies no inspectable source for the broader optimization-to-saddle boundary claim.

children.title: Nash Equilibria as VIs
children.top_down_role: VI formulations for strategic equilibrium systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Nash Equilibria as VIs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional differentiable convex games with uncoupled feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X:=\prod_{i=1}^N X_i\) and define
\[
F(x):=\bigl(\nabla_{x_1}J_1(x),\ldots,\nabla_{x_N}J_N(x)\bigr).
\]
A profile \(x^*\in X\) is a Nash equilibrium,
\[
J_i(x_i^*,x_{-i}^*)\leq J_i(x_i,x_{-i}^*)
\quad\text{for every }x_i\in X_i\text{ and }i=1,\ldots,N,
\]
if and only if
\[
\langle F(x^*),x-x^*\rangle\geq0
\quad\text{for every }x\in X.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a differentiable convex game with product constraints, Nash equilibria are exactly the solutions of the pseudo-gradient VI.
assumptions_latex: For \(i=1,\ldots,N\), the strategy set \(X_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_i}\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
Each \(J_i\) is continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(X:=\prod_{i=1}^N X_i\).
For every fixed \(x_{-i}\), the function \(x_i\mapsto J_i(x_i,x_{-i})\) is convex on \(X_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A profile is a Nash equilibrium exactly when it solves \(\operatorname{VI}(X,F)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cournot Oligopoly First-Order Conditions as a Variational Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-cone generalized-equation representation of firms' first-order conditions, with own-output concavity required for equivalence to Cournot optimal-response conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let N=\{1,\ldots,n\}, let each Y_i\subset\mathbb R_+ be a nonempty closed interval, set Y=\prod_{i=1}^nY_i and T=\sum_{i=1}^ny_i, and define u_i(y)=y_ip(T)-f_i(y_i). Then the firms' first-order conditions can be written as 0\in-\mathcal M(y)+N_Y(y), where \mathcal M_i(y)=\nabla_{y_i}u_i(y)=p(T)+y_ip'(T)-f_i'(y_i). If each u_i(\cdot,y_{-i}) is concave on Y_i, this generalized equation is equivalent to the firms' individual optimal-response conditions and hence characterizes Cournot equilibria.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The firms' first-order conditions form a normal-cone generalized equation whose mapping is marginal profit. If every firm's profit is concave in its own output, this system is equivalent to the firms' optimal-response conditions and characterizes Cournot equilibrium. Convex costs contribute the cost-side concavity but do not alone establish profit concavity.
assumptions_latex: N=\{1,\ldots,n\},\quad Y_i\subset\mathbb R_+\text{ is a nonempty closed interval for every }i
\text{For equivalence to optimal-response conditions, }u_i(\cdot,y_{-i})\text{ is concave on }Y_i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in-\mathcal M(y)+N_Y(y),\qquad \mathcal M_i(y)=p(T)+y_ip'(T)-f_i'(y_i),\quad\text{and under own-output concavity this characterizes Cournot equilibrium.}

children.title: Network Equilibria as VIs
children.top_down_role: VI formulations for flow, traffic, and network equilibrium systems.

assumptions_latex: A directed network has a nonempty closed convex feasible flow set \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^A\).
The arc-cost map \(c:K\to\mathbb R^A\) is continuous.
Users are nonatomic and select feasible routes of minimum experienced cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible flow is a Wardrop equilibrium exactly when it solves \(\operatorname{VI}(K,c)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static nonatomic routing equilibrium in arc-flow form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) encode flow conservation, nonnegativity, and fixed origin-destination demands. A feasible flow \(x^*\in K\) is a Wardrop equilibrium when every used route has minimum cost among routes serving the same demand pair. In aggregate arc-flow variables this equilibrium condition is equivalent to
\[
\langle c(x^*),x-x^*\rangle
=\sum_{a\in A}c_a(x^*)(x_a-x_a^*)\geq0
\quad\text{for every }x\in K.
\]
Thus the network equilibrium is represented by \(\operatorname{VI}(K,c)\); uniqueness of the aggregate flow additionally follows when \(c\) is strictly monotone on \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Wardrop traffic equilibrium is the VI asserting that no feasible aggregate flow has lower cost in the equilibrium cost vector.
knowledge_statements.title: Network Equilibria as VIs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied, and the route-based Wardrop condition requires explicit assumptions connecting route costs, arc costs, feasible path flows, and aggregate arc flows. The strict-monotonicity uniqueness claim also requires source support.

children.title: Network Games as VI Models
children.top_down_role: VI models combining strategic interaction with network structure.

assumptions_latex: Player \(i\) chooses a network action \(x_i\) from a nonempty closed convex set, with joint feasible set \(K\).
Each cost \(J_i(x_i,x_{-i})\) is differentiable and convex in the player's own action.
Shared network effects enter the costs or the joint feasible constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every variational network equilibrium solves the VI on \(K\) induced by the game pseudo-gradient.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex differentiable network games, including shared constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
F(x):=\bigl(\nabla_{x_1}J_1(x),\ldots,\nabla_{x_N}J_N(x)\bigr).
\]
A variational network equilibrium is a point \(x^*\in K\) satisfying
\[
\langle F(x^*),x-x^*\rangle
=\sum_i\left\langle\nabla_{x_i}J_i(x^*),x_i-x_i^*\right\rangle\geq0
\quad\text{for every }x\in K.
\]
When \(K=\prod_iX_i\), this condition is equivalent to Nash equilibrium under own-action convexity. For shared constraints, it selects the generalized Nash equilibria whose players use a common multiplier for the shared constraint system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex network game is modeled by the VI of its pseudo-gradient; shared constraints select the common-multiplier variational equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.title: Network Games as VI Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The product-set VI model is standard, but the shared-constraint claim about generalized Nash equilibria and common multipliers depends on a precise variational-equilibrium definition and constraint qualification. No inspectable source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: VIs as Equilibrium Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional optimization with a parameterized VI constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An optimization problem with a variational-inequality equilibrium constraint has the form
\[
\operatorname*{minimize}_{x,y}\ \Phi(x,y)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
x\in X,
\quad y\in K(x),
\quad \langle F(x,y),v-y\rangle\geq0\quad\text{for every }v\in K(x).
\]
Equivalently, its equilibrium constraint may be written as
\[
0\in F(x,y)+N_{K(x)}(y)
\]
or as \(y\in\operatorname{SOL}(K(x),F(x,\cdot))\). This equilibrium condition is part of the feasible-set definition of the upper-level problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper-level optimization problem has a VI equilibrium constraint when its lower-level variable is required to solve a parameterized VI.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the upper-level feasible set.
For every \(x\in X\), \(K(x)\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(F:X\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m\) defines the lower-level equilibrium field.
\(\Phi:X\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) is the upper-level objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lower-level constraint requires \(y\in\operatorname{SOL}(K(x),F(x,\cdot))\), producing an optimization problem with a VI equilibrium constraint.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Face-normal polyhedral decomposition associated with projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covering of the ambient space by face-normal cells and the common-face structure of their intersections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\). For the faces \(\mathcal F_I\) of \(P(A,b)\) and their associated cones \(\mathcal N_I\), \[\mathbb{R}^n=\bigcup_{I\in\mathcal I(A,b)}(\mathcal F_I+\mathcal N_I).\] If distinct \(I,J\in\mathcal I(A,b)\) satisfy \[P_{IJ}:=(\mathcal F_I+\mathcal N_I)\cap(\mathcal F_J+\mathcal N_J)\neq\varnothing,\] then \[P_{IJ}=(\mathcal F_I\cap\mathcal F_J)+(\mathcal N_I+\mathcal N_J),\] and \(P_{IJ}\) is a common face of \(\mathcal F_I+\mathcal N_I\) and \(\mathcal F_J+\mathcal N_J\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sums of each polyhedral face with its associated normal cone cover the ambient space. Whenever two distinct cells intersect, their intersection is the sum of the face intersection and the two associated normal cones, and is a common face of both cells.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb{R}^n=\bigcup_{I\in\mathcal I(A,b)}(\mathcal F_I+\mathcal N_I);\quad P_{IJ}\neq\varnothing\Rightarrow P_{IJ}=(\mathcal F_I\cap\mathcal F_J)+(\mathcal N_I+\mathcal N_J)\text{ and }P_{IJ}\text{ is a common face of both cells}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection, critical face, and critical cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records general closed-convex projection properties and defines the critical face and critical cone in the polyhedral specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Its Euclidean projection \(\operatorname{Proj}_\Omega\) is globally Lipschitz with constant \(1\), and \(y=\operatorname{Proj}_\Omega(x)\) if and only if \(x-y\in N_\Omega(y)\). If, additionally, \(\Omega\) is polyhedral and \(y=\operatorname{Proj}_\Omega(x)\), define \[F:=\{c\in\Omega:\langle x-y,c-y\rangle=0\}\] and \[K:=T_\Omega(y)\cap\{x-y\}^{\perp}.\] Then \(F\) is the critical face exposed by \(x-y\), and \(K=T_F(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a nonempty closed convex set is nonexpansive and is characterized by a normal-cone inclusion. For a polyhedral set, the projection residual exposes a critical face, and the corresponding critical cone equals the tangent cone to that face.
assumptions_latex: \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
\Omega\text{ is polyhedral for the critical-face and critical-cone conclusions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Lip}(\operatorname{Proj}_\Omega)\le 1,\quad y=\operatorname{Proj}_\Omega(x)\iff x-y\in N_\Omega(y),\quad F=\{c\in\Omega:\langle x-y,c-y\rangle=0\},\quad K=T_\Omega(y)\cap\{x-y\}^{\perp}=T_F(y).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local critical-cone formula for polyhedral projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An exact local representation of projection onto a polyhedral set around a reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be polyhedral, \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(y=\operatorname{Proj}_\Omega(x)\). Let \(K:=T_\Omega(y)\cap\{x-y\}^{\perp}\) be the associated critical cone. Then there exists a neighborhood \(U\) of \(0\) such that, for every \(k\in U\), \[\operatorname{Proj}_\Omega(x+k)=y+\operatorname{Proj}_K(k).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Locally, projection onto a polyhedral set equals the reference projection plus projection of the perturbation onto the associated critical cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists U\ni0\ \forall k\in U:\quad \operatorname{Proj}_\Omega(x+k)=y+\operatorname{Proj}_K(k).

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.

notation.meaning: Euclidean projector onto the convex set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection onto a closed convex set in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\), there is a unique point
\[
P_C(z):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\|x-z\|.
\]
For \(x\in C\), the following conditions are equivalent:
\[
x=P_C(z),
\qquad z-x\in N_C(x),
\qquad \langle z-x,y-x\rangle\leq0\quad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
Moreover, for all \(z,w\in\mathbb R^n\), the projector is firmly nonexpansive:
\[
\|P_Cz-P_Cw\|^2\leq\langle P_Cz-P_Cw,z-w\rangle.
\]
In particular, \(P_C\) is nonexpansive and hence globally Lipschitz with constant one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a closed convex set is unique, firmly nonexpansive, and characterized by the residual belonging to the normal cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Projector Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection characterization and firm nonexpansiveness property are mathematically correct and the property kind fits the geometry leaf, but no inspectable authoritative source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Euclidean Projection onto a Closed Convex Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closest-point definition and minimization representation of the Euclidean projector; nonemptiness is required for the asserted existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. For \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the Euclidean projection of \(x\) onto \(K\) is the unique closest point \[\Pi_K(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in K}\frac12\|y-x\|_2^2.\] The mapping \(\Pi_K:\mathbb{R}^n\to K\) is the Euclidean projector onto \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Euclidean projection onto a nonempty closed convex set is the unique point in the set minimizing squared Euclidean distance to the given point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi_K(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in K}\frac12\|y-x\|_2^2\text{ exists and is unique.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise structure of Euclidean projectors and the natural and normal maps induced by a polyhedral set and a matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a polyhedral set. Then \(\Pi_K\) is piecewise affine on \(\mathbb{R}^n\); if \(K\) is a polyhedral cone, \(\Pi_K\) is piecewise linear. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fundamental Properties of Euclidean Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence, variational characterization, firm nonexpansiveness, nonexpansiveness, and squared-distance smoothness for projection onto a nonempty closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Then: (i) \(\Pi_K(x)\) exists uniquely for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\); (ii) \(\bar x=\Pi_K(x)\) if and only if \(\bar x\in K\) and \[(y-\bar x)^T(\bar x-x)\ge0\quad\forall y\in K;\] (iii) for all \(u,v\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[(\Pi_K(u)-\Pi_K(v))^T(u-v)\ge\|\Pi_K(u)-\Pi_K(v)\|_2^2,\] hence \[\|\Pi_K(u)-\Pi_K(v)\|_2\le\|u-v\|_2;\] and (iv) \[\rho(x):=\frac12\|x-\Pi_K(x)\|_2^2\] is continuously differentiable with \(\nabla\rho(x)=x-\Pi_K(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a nonempty closed convex set exists uniquely, has a variational-inequality characterization, is firmly nonexpansive and therefore nonexpansive, and produces a continuously differentiable squared-distance function whose gradient is the projection residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi_K\text{ is single-valued and firmly nonexpansive, and }\rho(x)=\frac12\|x-\Pi_K(x)\|_2^2\in C^1(\mathbb{R}^n)\text{ with }\nabla\rho(x)=x-\Pi_K(x).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Face-indexed normal manifold of a polyhedral convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each nonempty face \(F\in\mathcal F(C)\), let \(N_C(F)\) denote the normal cone \(N_C(x)\) at any \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\), and define
\[
M_F:=F+N_C(F).
\]
The collection \(\{M_F:F\in\mathcal F(C)\}\) covers \(\mathbb R^n\), and the relative interiors of its full-dimensional cells are pairwise disjoint. If \(z\in M_F\), then \(P_C(z)\in F\); on every cell \(M_F\), the Euclidean projector \(P_C\) agrees with an affine mapping. Thus the face-normal pairs of \(C\) induce a polyhedral subdivision on which projection, and consequently a polyhedral normal map, is piecewise affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each face plus its normal cone forms a normal-manifold cell; these cells cover space and make polyhedral projection piecewise affine.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Manifold Decomposition

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K(p)\) be the parametric constraint set defined by (4.7.1), and suppose each \(g_i(\cdot,p)\) is convex for every \(p\in\mathcal P\). Fix \(p^*\in\mathcal P\), \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(x^*=\Pi_{K(p^*)}(x)\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: MFCQ yields sequential inner stability of a parametric feasible set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise feasible-set stability under perturbations of smooth inequality-and-equality constraints. The unidentified condition (4.7.2) is not interpreted beyond the explicit sequential conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\subset\mathbb R^p\) be open, let \(g:\mathbb R^n\times\mathcal P\to\mathbb R^m\) and \(h:\mathbb R^n\times\mathcal P\to\mathbb R^\ell\) be continuously differentiable, and define \(K(p)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g(x,p)\leq0,\ h(x,p)=0\}\). If MFCQ holds at \(x^*\in K(p^*)\), then for every sequence \(p^k\to p^*\), there exists a sequence \(x^k\to x^*\) such that \(x^k\in K(p^k)\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under MFCQ at a reference feasible point, every convergent sequence of parameter perturbations admits feasible points converging to that reference point.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall p^k\to p^*\;\exists x^k\to x^*\text{ such that }x^k\in K(p^k)\text{ for every }k.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Piecewise linear mappings and extended-real-valued functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional definition using a finite polyhedral cover and an affine formula on each piece; “piecewise linear” here permits affine offsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mapping \(F:D\to\mathbb R^m\), with \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\), is piecewise linear on \(D\) if \(D=\bigcup_{k=1}^N D_k\) for finitely many polyhedral sets \(D_k\) and, for each \(k\), there exist \(A_k\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(a_k\in\mathbb R^m\) such that \(F(x)=A_kx+a_k\) for every \(x\in D_k\). A function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is piecewise linear if its finite-valued restriction \(f:\operatorname{dom}f\to\mathbb R\) is piecewise linear in this sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mapping is piecewise linear when its domain has a finite polyhedral cover and it is affine on every member of that cover. An extended-real-valued function is piecewise linear when its restriction to its effective domain has this property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is piecewise linear on }D\iff\exists\{D_k,A_k,a_k\}_{k=1}^N:\ D=\bigcup_{k=1}^N D_k,\ D_k\text{ polyhedral},\ F(x)=A_kx+a_k\ \forall x\in D_k;\qquad f\text{ is piecewise linear}\iff f|_{\operatorname{dom}f}:\operatorname{dom}f\to\mathbb R\text{ is piecewise linear}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A block-matrix characterization for a piecewise-linear map involving a componentwise minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=\begin{bmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{bmatrix}\) be square, with \(A\) and \(D\) square, and define \(\Phi(u,v)=(Au+Bv,\,\min\{v,Cu+Dv\})\), where the minimum is componentwise. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global invertibility characterizations for piecewise-affine maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent global topological and orientation conditions for square piecewise-affine maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be piecewise affine. The following are equivalent: \(f\) is a homeomorphism; \(f\) is a Lipschitz homeomorphism; \(f\) is injective; \(f\) is bijective; and \(f\) is coherently oriented with \(\operatorname{ind}(f,x)\) well defined and equal to the same constant for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), this constant being \(1\) or \(-1\). If these conditions hold, then \(f^{-1}\) is piecewise affine and has the same properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a piecewise-affine self-map of Euclidean space, homeomorphism, Lipschitz homeomorphism, injectivity, bijectivity, and coherent orientation with constant index plus or minus one are equivalent. Its inverse is also piecewise affine and has the same properties.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (a)\Longleftrightarrow(b)\Longleftrightarrow(c)\Longleftrightarrow(d)\Longleftrightarrow(e),\qquad f^{-1}\text{ is piecewise affine and satisfies the same properties}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Piecewise affine and piecewise linear maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-piece definition for continuous vector-valued maps between Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuous map \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is piecewise affine (respectively, piecewise linear) if there exist finitely many affine (respectively, linear) maps \(f^1,\ldots,f^k:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), where \(k\geq1\), such that \[f(x)\in\{f^1(x),\ldots,f^k(x)\}\qquad\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] Each \(f^i\) is a piece of \(f\). In the piecewise-linear case, when \(f^i(x)=A^ix\) with \(A^i\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), the matrices \(A^1,\ldots,A^k\) are the linear pieces of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous vector-valued map is piecewise affine or piecewise linear when its value at every point agrees with one member of a fixed finite family of affine or linear maps. Those maps, and the corresponding matrices in the linear case, are its pieces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is PA (PL)}\iff \exists f^1,\ldots,f^k\text{ affine (linear) such that }f(x)\in\{f^1(x),\ldots,f^k(x)\}\ \forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Locally Piecewise Continuously Differentiable Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local finite-selection definition of a PC1 map, including its smooth pieces and active-index set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuous map $G:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is $PC^1$ near $x\in\mathcal D$ if there exist an open neighborhood $\mathcal N\subseteq\mathcal D$ of $x$, a positive integer $k$, and maps $G^1,\ldots,G^k\in C^1(\mathcal N;\mathbb R^m)$ such that $G(y)\in\{G^1(y),\ldots,G^k(y)\}$ for every $y\in\mathcal N$. Each $G^i$ is a $C^1$ piece of $G$ at $x$, and $\mathcal P(y):=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}:G(y)=G^i(y)\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous map is PC1 near a point if, on an open neighborhood of that point, it selects its value from a finite family of continuously differentiable maps. Those maps are its C1 pieces, and the active-index set records which pieces agree with the map at each argument.
assumptions_latex: G:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\text{ is continuous}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is }PC^1\text{ near }x\iff \exists\,\mathcal N\subseteq\mathcal D,\ k\in\mathbb N_{>0},\ G^1,\ldots,G^k\in C^1(\mathcal N;\mathbb R^m)\text{ such that }\forall y\in\mathcal N,\ G(y)\in\{G^1(y),\ldots,G^k(y)\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Piecewise-C1 Projection onto a Parametric Inequality Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth local projection branches associated with active equality manifolds furnish a piecewise-C1 representation of the projection onto the parameterized inequality set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the setting of Theorem 4.2.16, let \(\bar v=\bar y-F(\bar x,\bar y)\) and \(C^j(x)=\{y\in\mathbb R^m:g_i(x,y)=0\text{ for }i\in\mathcal I^j\}\). For each \(j=1,\ldots,J\), there are neighborhoods \(U\times W\) of \((\bar x,\bar v)\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\) such that every \((x,v)\in U\times W\) has a unique nearest point \(\Pi^j(x,v)\) in \(C^j(x)\cap V\), with \(\Pi^j(\bar x,\bar v)=\bar y\), and \(\Pi^j\) is locally \(C^1\). Moreover, \((x,v)\mapsto\Pi_{C(x)}(v)\) is locally \(PC^1\), with \(C^1\) pieces \(\Pi^j\), \(j=1,\ldots,J\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near the reference pair, projection onto every relevant equality manifold is uniquely defined and smooth, and these finitely many branches form a piecewise-C1 representation of projection onto the original inequality set.
assumptions_latex: The setting and hypotheses of Theorem 4.2.16 hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi^j\text{ is locally single-valued and }C^1,\quad \Pi^j(\bar x,\bar v)=\bar y,\quad ((x,v)\mapsto\Pi_{C(x)}(v))\in PC^1\text{ locally with pieces }\Pi^j.\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fréchet differentiability characterized through the critical cone and VI nondegeneracy, with additional equivalent conditions when the base point is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a polyhedron and \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). The following are equivalent: (a) \(\Pi_K\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(x\); (b) \(\mathcal C_\pi(x;K)\) is a linear subspace; and (c) \(\Pi_K(x)\) is a nondegenerate solution of \(\operatorname{VI}(K,\mathbf I-x)\). If the point lies in the polyhedron, tangent-cone linearity and relative-interior membership of zero in the normal cone are equivalent as well.
